cattle.hook: The world’s main meat-and-milk bovine: taurine and indicine cattle that people keep for milk, meat, hides, and draft.
cattle.imageAlt: Hereford cattle standing in a pasture
cattle.what: Cattle are domestic bovines kept for milk, meat, hides, and draft. Living cattle belong to the taurine (Bos taurus) and indicine (Bos indicus, zebu) lineages. People bred them from aurochs (Bos primigenius) in the Holocene.
cattle.range: Kept on every inhabited continent. Density follows pasture, feed, and dairy markets. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations maps the global distribution of cattle as livestock.
cattle.story: People domesticated cattle from aurochs in the Holocene and then moved the herds with farms and trade. Today the animal is a managed food system: breeds, feedlots, and pastoral herds.
cattle.when: A living domesticate, maintained by people worldwide.
cattle.humanRole: We made the animal, spread it, and now run the herds that feed much of the world.
cattle.sourcesNote: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, Livestock Systems: cattle.

chicken.hook: The most abundant domestic livestock: a junglefowl turned into the world’s default farm bird.
chicken.imageAlt: A domestic chicken standing in dry grass
chicken.what: The chicken (Gallus gallus domesticus) is the domestic form of the red junglefowl. It is the most abundant domestic livestock: more individual chickens are alive than any other farmed bird or mammal. People keep this bird for meat and eggs.
chicken.range: Villages, barns, and industrial houses on every inhabited continent. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations maps the global distribution of chickens as livestock.
chicken.story: Domestication in Asia produced a bird people could move. Industrial breeding then made meat and egg lines that live short, dense lives. Village flocks still exist beside the industrial houses.
chicken.when: A living domesticate, and the most numerous farm animal.
chicken.humanRole: We bred, housed, and counted them as a food system of meat and eggs.
chicken.sourcesNote: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, Livestock Systems: chickens.

sheep.hook: Sheep are grazing animals raised mainly for wool, meat, milk and hides, in breeds adapted to places from the cold, wet highlands of northern Europe to the dry lands of Africa, Asia and Australasia.
sheep.imageAlt: A domestic sheep standing in grass, facing the camera
sheep.what: The sheep (Ovis aries) is a domestic small ruminant kept for wool, meat, and milk.
sheep.range: Pastures from dry steppe to wet temperate hills, and feed systems beside them. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations maps the global distribution of sheep as livestock.
sheep.story: People domesticated sheep in the Neolithic Near East and walked them across continents. Breeds now fit wool, milk, or meat.
sheep.when: A living domesticate, raised for wool, meat, and milk.
sheep.humanRole: We bred and moved them as fibre and food; the landscape they graze is one we made.
sheep.sourcesNote: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, Livestock Systems: sheep.

pig.hook: The domestic pig, Sus domesticus, raised for meat on farms from village sties to industrial houses.
pig.imageAlt: A domestic pig in a farm yard, pink-skinned and heavy
pig.what: The pig (Sus domesticus) is the domestic pig people keep for meat. People domesticated pigs more than once from wild boar, and today most meat pigs are commercial lines. Village pigs and heritage breeds remain. Released and escaped animals have formed feral populations in many countries.
pig.range: Farms worldwide, from village sties to industrial houses. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations maps the global distribution of pigs as livestock.
pig.story: Pigs were domesticated more than once from wild boar. Today most meat pigs are commercial lines. Village pigs and heritage breeds remain, and released or escaped animals have formed feral populations in many countries.
pig.when: A living domesticate, raised for meat.
pig.humanRole: We keep them as food, and released or escaped animals have formed feral populations in many countries.
pig.sourcesNote: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, Livestock Systems: pigs.

water-buffalo.hook: About 15 percent of the world’s milk, and in India and Pakistan, more buffalo milk than cow milk.
water-buffalo.imageAlt: A domestic water buffalo bull near Mehsana, Gujarat, India
water-buffalo.what: The water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis) is the domestic Asian buffalo, kept for milk, meat, and draft. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations puts buffaloes at about 15 percent of world milk; in India and Pakistan buffalo milk exceeds cow milk.
water-buffalo.range: South and Southeast Asia hold most of the herd; smaller populations live in the Mediterranean, the Caucasus, South America, and elsewhere. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations maps buffaloes as livestock.
water-buffalo.story: People domesticated the Asian buffalo and built wet-rice and dairy systems around it. River and swamp types differ in milk, draft, and the wetlands they live in.
water-buffalo.when: A living domesticate, and a major dairy species in South Asia.
water-buffalo.humanRole: We keep buffaloes as milk and draft animals in South Asia and in smaller herds elsewhere.
water-buffalo.sourcesNote: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, buffalo dairy page and Livestock Systems: buffaloes.

horse.hook: Domestic horses spread from the Western Eurasian steppes around 2200-2000 BC, according to Librado and colleagues in Nature, 2021.
horse.imageAlt: A white Camargue horse standing in grass
horse.what: The horse (Equus ferus caballus) is the domestic horse people ride, drive, and keep. Work on ancient genetic material by Librado and colleagues (Nature, 2021) places the rise and spread of the modern domestic lineage on the Western Eurasian steppes, expanding around 2200-2000 BC. Horses from Botai in Kazakhstan belong to another lineage.
horse.range: Kept worldwide. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations maps horses as livestock. Working, sport, and feral herds live on every inhabited continent.
horse.story: The modern domestic lineage replaced earlier lineages as it spread with people. That date is a genetic result from a 2021 study. Working, sport, and feral herds descend from that kept lineage.
horse.when: A living domesticate. Modern lineage: Western Eurasian steppes, around 2200-2000 BC (Librado and colleagues, 2021).
horse.humanRole: We bred and moved them as transport and work. The date of the living lineage comes from a 2021 genetic study.
horse.sourcesNote: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, Livestock Systems: horses; Librado and colleagues, Nature, 2021 (doi:10.1038/s41586-021-04018-9).

dog.hook: The first domestic animal, already genetically distinct from present-day wolves, with at least five lineages by about 11,000 years ago.
dog.imageAlt: Two black Labrador retrievers with collars in dry grass
dog.what: The dog (Canis familiaris) is the first animal people domesticated. Bergström and colleagues (Science, 2020) show that dogs were already genetically distinct from present-day wolves, and that at least five dog lineages existed by about 11,000 years ago.
dog.range: Wherever people live. Village dogs, working lines, and pedigree breeds are all the same domestic species.
dog.story: Dogs entered human camps in the Late Pleistocene. By the early Holocene they were already a set of lineages, genetically distinct from present-day wolves. Later breeding made the modern types.
dog.when: The oldest domesticate. Distinct from present-day wolves by the Holocene; at least five lineages by about 11,000 years ago (Bergström and colleagues, 2020).
dog.humanRole: We made the first kept animal: a companion, hunter, and guard.
dog.sourcesNote: Bergström and colleagues, Science, 2020 (full text in PubMed Central; doi:10.1126/science.aba9572).

camelids.hook: People keep dromedaries, Bactrian camels, llamas, and alpacas for transport, fibre, milk, and meat, and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations marked 2024 as the International Year of Camelids.
camelids.what: The camelids people keep are the dromedary and the Bactrian camel (Camelus), the llama (Lama glama), and the alpaca (Vicugna pacos). The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations marked 2024 as the International Year of Camelids.
camelids.range: Camels live in dry Asia and Africa, and now in Australia. Llamas and alpacas live in the Andes, with export herds elsewhere.
camelids.story: People domesticated Old World camels and Andean camelids as pack, fibre, milk, and meat animals of dry and high country. The 2024 International Year of Camelids asked governments to treat those herds as a food-and-culture system.
camelids.when: Living domesticates. The International Year of Camelids was 2024.
camelids.humanRole: We keep camels, llamas, and alpacas as working and fibre animals of dry and mountain lands.
camelids.sourcesNote: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, International Year of Camelids 2024.

goat.hook: A browsing small ruminant kept mainly for meat, milk, hides and hair on smallholder farms, in pastoral herds and on specialised dairy farms.
goat.imageAlt: A brown domestic goat with long, drooping ears.
goat.what: The domestic goat (Capra hircus; the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, FAO, writes Capra aegagrus hircus) is a small ruminant that people keep mainly for meat, milk, hides and hair. Goats are mainly browsers with an extremely varied plant diet, and this has let them adapt to many different environments.
goat.range: Goats are widely distributed and are raised in a wide range of farming systems around the world. Most live on smallholder mixed farms. Goats are also an important part of pastoralist herds, and high-value animals are kept for specialised dairy production in temperate regions. FAO publishes global maps of goats per square kilometre for 2010, 2015 and 2020.
goat.story: Goats were among the first hoofed animals that people domesticated. Archaeological evidence traces goat domestication back about 10,500 years, to the upper Euphrates valley in southeastern Anatolia. A study of 473 wild bezoar goats, the domestic goat's wild ancestor (Naderi and colleagues, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2008), found that almost all domestic goats today probably come from a domestication centre in eastern Anatolia that may also have reached the northern and central Zagros mountains.
goat.when: A living domesticate raised worldwide. FAO's Domestic Animal Diversity Information System (DAD-IS) records livestock breeds and their risk of extinction; it covers around 8,800 breeds of 38 species.
goat.humanRole: People keep goats for milk, meat, hides and hair on family farms, in herds that move with pastoralists and on dairy farms.

sources.label: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO): Livestock Systems, Goats

Saeid Naderi et al.: The goat domestication process inferred from large-scale mitochondrial DNA analysis of wild and domestic individuals, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2008 (full text in PubMed Central)

cat.hook: A companion and pest hunter descended from the Near Eastern wildcat, whose bond with people began more than 9,000 years ago around the grain stores of the first farmers.
cat.imageAlt: A young tabby cat in Portugal.
cat.what: The domestic cat (Felis catus) lives in homes and on farms as a companion and as a guard against pests. It descends from the Near Eastern wildcat (Felis silvestris lybica).
cat.range: People have carried cats all over the world, and the domestic cat may be the world's most numerous pet. House cats, farm cats, pedigree breeds and free-roaming town cats all descend from the same Near Eastern ancestors.
cat.story: A genetic study of 979 domestic cats and wildcats (Driscoll and colleagues, Science, 2007) found that cats were domesticated in the Near East, probably as farming villages grew in the Fertile Crescent, and that they descend from at least five founders. Ancient DNA (Ottoni and colleagues, Nature Ecology & Evolution, 2017) shows that both Near Eastern and Egyptian wildcat populations contributed to the domestic cat: the spread began in the Neolithic in the Near East and gained pace in the Classical period, when Egyptian cats spread throughout the Old World along sea and land trade routes. One coat-colour variant became common only after the Middle Ages, which suggests that people began breeding cats for their looks later than most other domestic animals.
cat.when: A living domesticate, kept as a companion animal worldwide.
cat.humanRole: Wildcats probably first settled near people by hunting the rodents that infested the grain stores of early farmers. People later carried cats on ships and along trade roads across the Old World.

sources.label: Claudio Ottoni et al.: The palaeogenetics of cat dispersal in the ancient world, Nature Ecology & Evolution, 2017
Carlos A. Driscoll et al.: The Near Eastern Origin of Cat Domestication, Science, 2007 (full text in PubMed Central)

donkey.hook: A beast of burden domesticated in Africa around 5000 BCE; 99% of the world's donkeys live in low- and middle-income countries.
donkey.imageAlt: A donkey grazing at Clovelly, North Devon, England.
donkey.what: The domestic donkey (Equus asinus) is a working animal that carries loads and people over long distances, especially across semi-arid and upland country. It remains a key support for many households in low- and middle-income countries.
donkey.range: The charity Brooke, which works to improve the lives of working horses, donkeys and mules, estimates that there are about 116 million equines (donkeys, horses and mules) in the world, about 36 million of them in the 38 lowest-income countries, and that 99% of the world's donkeys live in low- and middle-income countries. Many countries lack accurate population data: of 36 countries whose latest censuses Brooke reviewed, 22 had not counted their equines in the previous 10 years.
donkey.story: A study of the genomes of 207 modern and 31 ancient donkeys and 15 wild equines (Todd and colleagues, Science, 2022) supports a single domestication in Africa around 5000 BCE, followed by expansions across Africa and Eurasia. An earlier study of 126 domestic donkeys and seven wild asses (Wang and colleagues, Nature Communications, 2020) also points to Africa. It found low genetic variety on the Y chromosome, which probably reflects how people managed breeding, and showed that the undiluted black or chestnut coats of domestic donkeys were probably established during domestication.
donkey.when: A living domesticate and working animal. The Domestic Animal Diversity Information System (DAD-IS) of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) records donkey breeds. Brooke asks governments to classify working donkeys, horses and mules as livestock so that national livestock censuses count them.
donkey.humanRole: Donkeys have carried goods over long distances for thousands of years, and they still support the livelihoods of many communities.

sources.label: Evelyn T. Todd et al.: The genomic history and global expansion of domestic donkeys, Science, 2022 (bibliographic record, LMU Munich; DOI: 10.1126/science.abo3503)
Changfa Wang et al.: Donkey genomes provide new insights into domestication and selection for coat color, Nature Communications, 2020 (full text in PubMed Central)

duck.hook: Farm ducks, most of them descended from mallards first domesticated in Southeast Asia at least 4,000 years ago, raised for meat, eggs and feathers where water is plentiful.
duck.imageAlt: Domestic ducks in the paddy fields near Ubud, Bali, Indonesia.
duck.what: Farm ducks are raised for meat, eggs and feathers. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), most farmed ducks descend from the mallard (Anas platyrhynchos). Breeds vary greatly with place and with whether they were bred for meat, eggs, feathers or several purposes at once.
duck.range: Ducks are most numerous in areas with abundant water. FAO notes particularly large numbers in Bangladesh, China and Southeast Asia; ducks are also popular in Egypt, Nigeria and much of Europe, especially western France. FAO publishes global maps of ducks per square kilometre for 2010 and 2015.
duck.story: People first domesticated ducks from mallards in Southeast Asia at least 4,000 years ago. Today ducks are raised in many kinds of farming, from a few birds on a mixed farm to vast flocks taken by lorry to paddy fields to clear them after the rice harvest.
duck.when: A living domesticate. FAO's Domestic Animal Diversity Information System (DAD-IS) records duck breeds.
duck.humanRole: Farmers keep ducks on ponds and mixed farms, and in rice-growing regions flocks feed in the paddies after the harvest.

sources.label: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO): Livestock Systems, Ducks
FAO: Domestic Animal Diversity Information System (DAD-IS)

rabbit.hook: Domesticated from the wild rabbit of southern Europe and North Africa by the late Middle Ages, and raised today for meat, fur and wool on farms and in backyards.
rabbit.imageAlt: A black domestic rabbit on straw at the Hirschstetten flower gardens in Vienna, Austria.
rabbit.what: The domestic rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus) is raised for meat, for skins used as fur and, in Angora rabbits, for wool. It descends from the wild rabbit of southern Europe and North Africa.
rabbit.range: Rabbit keeping in hutches spread across rural western Europe and into city suburbs, and European colonial expansion took rabbits to many countries where they had been unknown, such as Australia and New Zealand. Rabbits are now found in almost every climate. The rabbit manual of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) describes backyard rabbitries as well suited to small farmers, with or without land of their own.
rabbit.story: According to the FAO manual The Rabbit: Husbandry, health and production (1997), Phoenicians who reached the coast of Spain about 1000 BCE are thought to have discovered the wild rabbit. The Roman writer Varro (116-27 BCE) suggested keeping rabbits in leporaria, stone-walled pens or parks shared with hares and other wild animals for hunting; rabbits were still not domesticated then. Several breeds were known in the sixteenth century, the first sign of controlled breeding, so domestication is traced to the late Middle Ages, probably mainly the work of monks.
rabbit.when: A living domesticate. FAO's Domestic Animal Diversity Information System (DAD-IS) records rabbit breeds.
rabbit.humanRole: Fibrous feed is an important part of a rabbit's diet, so rabbits do not compete directly with people for food, and in efficient systems they turn 20% of the protein they eat into edible meat. This makes them useful to rural families who need more animal protein.

sources.label: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO): The Rabbit: Husbandry, health and production (Animal Production and Health Series No. 21, new revised version, 1997), PDF
